transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Mr. Lindqvist, thank you for coming back in today. I’ve reviewed your new labs and the recurrence of your symptoms, and I need to be honest with you about why this happened.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I can tell you already. The fever is back and the inflammation is exactly where it was three weeks ago. I told the nurse on the phone that the course didn't feel right.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: You were right. I made a mistake with your prescription. I prescribed the correct antibiotic and the correct dose, but I only gave you a seven-day supply when you actually needed fourteen. It was my error.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You’re joking. Seven days? For this specific infection? I spent ten years as a paramedic, I know the protocol for this. You didn't just miss a dose, you cut the treatment duration in half.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am incredibly sorry. I take full responsibility for this. I failed to double-check the duration against the guidelines for your specific diagnosis, and that is entirely on me.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Sorry doesn't fix the fact that I've spent the last three days shaking in bed again. I trusted you because we've worked together for a year. Now I'm back at square one because you couldn't count to fourteen?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand you're angry. It is completely unacceptable that you are suffering through these symptoms again because of my oversight.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Unacceptable is an understatement. This is clinical negligence. How does a doctor just forget the duration of a standard course? Were you just rushing through my chart?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: There is no excuse for it. I simply missed it, and I am deeply sorry for the pain and frustration this has caused you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So what now? Do I just take another seven days and hope you don't mess up the math again?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Let's look at the plan. I've already coordinated with the pharmacy to have a full fourteen-day course of the same medication ready for you now. You'll pick it up today. I want you to start the first dose immediately.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And if it doesn't take this time? Since the bacteria might have had a chance to build resistance because of the short course?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is a valid concern. Because of the interruption, we aren't just going to guess. I've ordered a repeat culture of the site today to ensure the pathogen is still susceptible to this specific agent. I'll have those results by Thursday morning.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm not just going to "wait and see" if I feel better this time.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand. To make sure we get this right, I want you to call my direct line every forty-eight hours for the first week. You tell me exactly how your temperature is and if the redness is receding. If there is any plateau in your progress, I will see you in person immediately.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I’ll do that, but I’m still not happy about this.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know. I can't take back the mistake, but I will make sure we monitor this every step of the way until you're fully recovered.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Fine. Thursday for the cultures.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Yes, Thursday. And I will personally call you the moment those results hit my desk.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You better.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I will. I'm going to go grab the printout of the new prescription and the lab order for you now. I'll be right back.

H.justification: Resident never interrupts the patient, remains regulated despite significant pushback, and avoids all rushing language.

E.justification: The error was named explicitly and in lay language, but the resident failed to perform any comprehension checks.

A.justification: Resident used direct apology language, took full personal responsibility, and maintained accountability throughout the patient's anger.

R.justification: Resident named specific emotions ('angry', 'frustration') and engaged with the patient's specific concerns regarding resistance and trust.

T.justification: Plan includes specific steps (new prescription, repeat culture), timelines (Thursday), patient role (call every 48 hours), and prevention (monitoring until recovery).
